learn: What part-of-speech tagging is and what it is used for
The Penn Treebank and Universal Dependencies tagsets
Why tag ambiguity makes tagging a sequence problem
Markov chains: states, start probabilities and transitions
Hidden Markov models: transition and emission probabilities and the joint probability
Estimating HMM parameters by counting a tagged corpus
A worked decision: tagging 'race' in 'to race tomorrow'
intro.why: Tagging is the classic sequence-labelling task. The HMM introduced here, a generative model that combines a prior over label sequences with per-label word likelihoods, is the template for named-entity recognition, speech recognition and many other problems, and sets up Viterbi decoding in M7.

sections.title: The tagging task and its uses
sections.plain: Label every word with its grammatical category, using the word and its context.
sections.body:
Part-of-speech (POS) tagging assigns each token a tag from a fixed tagset: a sequence labelling task (one label per input token). "the lead paint is unsafe" → the/DT lead/NN paint/NN is/VBZ unsafe/JJ. Here "lead" is a noun (the metal); in "lead the team" it would be a verb.

Uses: lemmatisation (knowing "saw" is a verb gives lemma "see", a noun gives "saw"), parsing (tags are the leaves of syntax trees, M9–M10), named-entity recognition (proper nouns), information extraction, text-to-speech (REcord noun vs reCORD verb), machine translation and word-sense disambiguation (M13).

Traditional grammar names about eight classes: noun, verb, pronoun, preposition, adverb, conjunction, adjective, article/determiner (often with interjection). Computational tagsets are larger and more precise.

sections.title: Open and closed word classes
sections.plain: Content-word classes keep growing; function-word classes are small and fixed.
sections.body:
Open classes accept new members readily: nouns (laptop, selfie), verbs (stream, google), adjectives (happy), adverbs (quickly). Closed classes are small, fixed sets of mostly short, very frequent function words: prepositions (of, on), determiners/articles (the, a), pronouns (she, it), auxiliaries and modals (can, will, is), conjunctions (and, because), particles.

Why it matters for tagging: an unknown word at test time is almost certainly from an open class, so a tagger can restrict guesses to noun/verb/adjective/adverb and use clues such as suffixes (-tion, -ly, -ed) and capitalisation. Closed-class words are known and frequent, but often ambiguous (that, can, to).

sections.title: Penn Treebank and Universal tagsets
sections.plain: Standard tag inventories: 45 detailed English tags, or 17 coarse tags shared across languages.
sections.body:
The Penn Treebank tagset (45 tags) is the long-standing English standard. Common tags: NN (singular noun), NNS (plural), NNP (proper), VB (base verb), VBD (past), VBG (gerund/participle), VBZ (3rd-person singular present), DT (determiner), JJ (adjective), RB (adverb), IN (preposition and subordinating conjunction), TO ("to"), MD (modal), PRP (pronoun).

Worked: "The/DT grand/JJ jury/NN commented/VBD on/IN a/DT number/NN of/IN other/JJ topics/NNS ./."

The Universal Dependencies (UD) tagset has 17 coarse tags (NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ADV, PRON, DET, ADP, AUX, CCONJ, SCONJ, PROPN, NUM, PART, INTJ, PUNCT, SYM, X) designed to be consistent across many languages; finer distinctions go into separate morphological features. The tagset choice changes accuracy figures, so compare taggers only on the same tagset.

sections.title: Tag ambiguity and the sequence explosion
sections.plain: Many frequent words have several possible tags; choosing tags one by one ignores how neighbouring tags constrain each other.
sections.body:
Most word types have one tag, but the ambiguous ones are common, so a large share of word tokens are ambiguous. "I can can the can": modal (MD), verb (VB), noun (NN). "back": JJ (the back door), NN (on my back), RB (win the voters back), VB (back the bill).

A simple most-frequent-tag baseline (tag each word with the tag it had most often in training) already reaches about 92% on English newspaper text; good sequence taggers reach about 97%. The remaining gain comes from context: after "to", a verb is likely; after "the", a noun or adjective.

The best tag sequence must be found jointly. With T tags and n words there are Tⁿ candidate sequences: 45⁵ ≈ 1.85 × 10⁸ for a five-word sentence. Enumeration is hopeless; the HMM's structure allows dynamic programming (Viterbi, M7) in O(T²n).

sections.title: Markov chains
sections.plain: A model of sequences where the next state depends only on the current state.
sections.body:
A Markov chain has states Q = q₁…q_N, a start distribution π (πᵢ = P(first state = i)) and a transition matrix A with $a_{ij} = P(q_t = j\mid q_{t-1} = i)$, each row summing to 1. The Markov assumption: $P(q_t\mid q_1\dots q_{t-1}) = P(q_t\mid q_{t-1})$. A bigram language model is a Markov chain over words.

Worked (weather states hot, cold, warm): with π(warm) = 0.2 and a(warm → warm) = 0.6, P(warm warm warm warm) = 0.2 × 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.0432.

In a Markov chain the states are observed. For tagging, we observe words, but the tags are hidden; that calls for a hidden Markov model.

sections.title: Hidden Markov models
sections.plain: Hidden tags follow a Markov chain; each tag emits a visible word.
sections.body:
An HMM adds an observation sequence and emission probabilities: transitions A (N × N, P(tag | previous tag)), emissions B (N × |V|, P(word | tag)), and start distribution π. Two assumptions: the Markov assumption on tags, and output independence, P(wᵢ) depends only on tᵢ. It is generative: it tells a story of how tags and words are produced.

$$P(w_{1:n}, t_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(t_i\mid t_{i-1})\,P(w_i\mid t_i)$$

Worked: "the dog barks" with tags DT NN VB: transitions 0.3 × 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.06; emissions 0.4 × 0.02 × 0.03 = 0.00024; joint 1.44 × 10⁻⁵.

Decoding by Bayes' rule: $\hat t_{1:n} = \arg\max_t P(t\mid w) = \arg\max_t P(w\mid t)P(t)$ (the denominator P(w) is the same for all tag sequences): likelihood × prior, i.e. maximum a posteriori (MAP). An ice-cream example makes the structure concrete: hidden weather (Hot/Cold) emits an observed number of ice creams eaten; for observations 3, 1, 3 there are 2³ = 8 weather paths, and HCH scores highest (0.0128).

sections.title: Estimating HMM probabilities
sections.plain: From a hand-tagged corpus, count tag bigrams and word–tag pairs and divide.
sections.body:
$$P(t_i\mid t_{i-1}) = \frac{C(t_{i-1}, t_i)}{C(t_{i-1})},\qquad P(w_i\mid t_i) = \frac{C(t_i, w_i)}{C(t_i)}$$

For example, if DT occurs 1000 times and is followed by NN 600 times, P(NN | DT) = 0.6; if VBZ occurs 500 times and 300 of them are "is", P(is | VBZ) = 0.6.

Worked toy corpus: "the/DT employees/NNS pass/VB an/DT exam/NN ./." · "the/DT employees/NNS wait/VB for/IN the/DT pass/VB ./." · "employers/NNS fire/VB employees/NNS ./.". Start: P(DT) = 2/3, P(NNS) = 1/3. DT occurs 4 times, followed by NNS twice, VB once, NN once: P(NNS | DT) = 1/2, P(VB | DT) = 1/4, P(NN | DT) = 1/4. Emissions: P(the | DT) = 3/4, P(exam | NN) = 1, P(employees | NNS) = 3/4. (The second sentence tags "the pass" as VB, an annotation error that the model would faithfully learn.)

Unseen transitions and word–tag pairs need smoothing (M4), and unknown words need suffix/capitalisation-based emission estimates.

sections.title: Worked example: tagging 'race'
sections.plain: The transition from 'to' outweighs the word's own preference for being a noun.
sections.body:
"Secretariat is expected to/TO race/? tomorrow/NR." Compare the two choices for "race", keeping the surrounding tags:

pathP(tag | TO)P(NR | tag)P(race | tag)product
VB0.830.00270.000122.7 × 10⁻⁷
NN0.000470.00120.000573.2 × 10⁻¹⁰

"race" on its own is more often a noun (0.00057 vs 0.00012), but a verb after "to" is overwhelmingly more likely (0.83 vs 0.00047), so the VB path wins by a factor of about 840. This is the HMM's prior × likelihood at work, and shows why per-word decisions fail.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• 97% is not "solved": with ~20-word sentences, a 97% tagger still makes an error in roughly half of all sentences.
  • Inter-annotator agreement on Penn tags is itself about 97%, an upper bound on what a tagger trained on those annotations can show.
  • Unsupervised HMMs can be trained with the forward–backward (Baum–Welch, EM) algorithm, but rarely recover linguistic tags exactly.
  • Trigram HMMs condition on two previous tags, as n-gram LMs do on words.

code.title: Tag ambiguity, Markov chain and HMM counts
code.explain: Shows ambiguous words and the 45⁵ ≈ 1.85 × 10⁸ search space, the Markov chain probability 0.0432, the HMM joint probability 1.44 × 10⁻⁵ for 'the dog barks', and maximum-likelihood start, transition and emission estimates from a three-sentence tagged corpus.
mistakes: Dividing transition counts by the number of sentences.
code.code:
"""Tag ambiguity, the sequence explosion, a Markov chain, and HMM estimation from a tiny tagged corpus."""
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from fractions import Fraction as F

# 1. Ambiguous words and the size of the search space
amb = {"can": ["MD", "VB", "NN"], "back": ["JJ", "NN", "RB", "VB"], "lead": ["NN", "VB"], "race": ["NN", "VB"]}
for w, t in amb.items():
    print(f"{w:5s} -> {', '.join(t)}")
print(f"45 tags, 5 words: 45**5 = {45**5:,} possible tag sequences")

# 2. Markov chain over weather states
pi = {"hot": 0.5, "cold": 0.3, "warm": 0.2}
A = {"warm": {"warm": 0.6, "hot": 0.3, "cold": 0.1}}
p = pi["warm"] * A["warm"]["warm"] ** 3  # start warm, then stay warm three times
print(f"P(warm warm warm warm) = 0.2 * 0.6^3 = {p:.4f}")

# 3. HMM joint probability of 'the dog barks' with tags DT NN VB
trans = [("<s>", "DT", 0.3), ("DT", "NN", 0.5), ("NN", "VB", 0.4)]
emis = [("the", "DT", 0.4), ("dog", "NN", 0.02), ("barks", "VB", 0.03)]
pt = 1; pe = 1
for a, b, q in trans: pt *= q
for w, t, q in emis: pe *= q
print(f"transitions {pt:.3f} x emissions {pe:.5f} = joint {pt*pe:.3g}")

# 4. Maximum-likelihood HMM estimates from a tagged corpus
corpus = ["the/DT employees/NNS pass/VB an/DT exam/NN ./.",
          "the/DT employees/NNS wait/VB for/IN the/DT pass/VB ./.",
          "employers/NNS fire/VB employees/NNS ./."]
tc, bc, ec, start = Counter(), Counter(), Counter(), Counter()
for s in corpus:
    toks = [x.rsplit("/", 1) for x in s.split()]
    start[toks[0][1]] += 1; prev = None
    for w, t in toks:
        tc[t] += 1; ec[(t, w)] += 1
        if prev: bc[(prev, t)] += 1
        prev = t
print("start:", {t: str(F(c, len(corpus))) for t, c in start.items()})
nxt = defaultdict(dict)
for (a, b), c in bc.items():
    nxt[a][b] = str(F(c, sum(v for (x, _), v in bc.items() if x == a)))
print("after DT:", nxt["DT"])
print("P(the|DT) =", F(ec[("DT", "the")], tc["DT"]), " P(exam|NN) =", F(ec[("NN", "exam")], tc["NN"]),
      " P(employees|NNS) =", F(ec[("NNS", "employees")], tc["NNS"]))

code.title: Tagging 'race' and enumerating HMM paths
code.explain: Compares the VB and NN paths for 'to race tomorrow' (≈ 840× in favour of VB), then scores all 8 hidden weather paths of an ice-cream HMM for observations 3, 1, 3 by brute force.
code.notes: Brute force grows as Tⁿ; M7 replaces it with Viterbi.
code.code:
"""Tagging 'race' with an HMM, and scoring every hidden path of a tiny weather/ice-cream HMM."""
from itertools import product

# 1. 'to race tomorrow' : VB or NN for 'race'?
p_vb = 0.83 * 0.0027 * 0.00012     # P(VB|TO) P(NR|VB) P(race|VB)
p_nn = 0.00047 * 0.0012 * 0.00057  # P(NN|TO) P(NR|NN) P(race|NN)
print(f"VB path: {p_vb:.2e}   NN path: {p_nn:.2e}   ratio ~ {p_vb/p_nn:.0f}x  -> tag race as VB")

# 2. Ice-cream HMM: hidden weather H/C, observed number of ice creams
pi = {"H": 0.8, "C": 0.2}
A = {"H": {"H": 0.6, "C": 0.4}, "C": {"H": 0.5, "C": 0.5}}
B = {"H": {1: 0.2, 2: 0.4, 3: 0.4}, "C": {1: 0.5, 2: 0.4, 3: 0.1}}
obs = [3, 1, 3]
rows = []
for path in product("HC", repeat=len(obs)):
    p = pi[path[0]] * B[path[0]][obs[0]]
    for t in range(1, len(obs)):
        p *= A[path[t-1]][path[t]] * B[path[t]][obs[t]]
    rows.append(("".join(path), p))
rows.sort(key=lambda r: -r[1])
for s, p in rows:
    print(f"{s}: {p:.5f}")
print(f"{len(rows)} paths (2^3); best = {rows[0][0]}; total P(observations) = {sum(p for _, p in rows):.5f}")
